extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduate / beginning graduate students and researchers learning algebraic topology
extracted.subtask_description: Develop and compute simplicial and singular homology groups for topological spaces (CW/ D-complexes, simplicial complexes, arbitrary spaces), including definitions (chains, boundaries), basic properties (exactness, invariance), and example calculations (S^n, S^1, torus, RP^2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental group low-dimensional dependence
rubrics_metrics.description: When X is a CW complex, π1(X) depends only on the 2-skeleton of X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reflects the low-dimensional nature of π1: its definition involves only maps from the interval and homotopies of loops (I and I×I). Use only the 2-skeleton when computing or reasoning about π1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Higher homotopy groups skeleton dependence
rubrics_metrics.description: For a CW complex X, the homotopy group πn(X) depends only on the (n+1)-skeleton of X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This generalizes the low-dimensional dependence of π1: maps In and homotopies In×I suffice, so cells above dimension n+1 do not affect πn.

rubrics_metrics.name: Homology skeleton dependence for CW complexes
rubrics_metrics.description: For a CW complex X, the homology group Hn(X) depends only on the (n+1)-skeleton of X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As with homotopy groups, homology is determined by a limited portion of the cell structure; this is used to reduce computations to finite skeleta.

rubrics_metrics.name: Homology as computable alternative to homotopy
rubrics_metrics.description: Homology groups Hn(X) provide a more computable substitute for homotopy groups πn(X), and for spheres Hi(S^n)=0 for i>n and often coincide with πi(S^n) in range 1≤i≤n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While πn(S^n)=Z and πi(S^n)=0 for i<n, higher homotopy groups are hard to compute; homology is easier and vanishes above the sphere's dimension, making it a practical invariant for many problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chain groups and boundary maps (cellular/simplicial viewpoint)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a cell complex X one has chain groups Cn(X), free abelian on the n-cells, and boundary homomorphisms ∂n : Cn(X)→Cn−1(X); homology is Hn(X)=Ker ∂n / Im ∂n+1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the core algebraic definition used for computations on CW/ D-complexes: list n-cells, form free abelian groups, compute ∂n from attaching maps (for n=1 easy; for n=2 manageable), then compute kernels/images and quotients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicial boundary formula and orientation convention
rubrics_metrics.description: For an ordered n-simplex [v0,...,vn], the boundary is ∂[v0,...,vn]=∑_{i}(-1)^i [v0,...,hat{vi},...,vn]; ordering of vertices determines orientations of faces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the vertex ordering to assign coherent orientations to faces. This alternating-sum formula is the concrete rule for computing boundaries in simplicial homology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chain complex condition (∂∘∂=0)
rubrics_metrics.description: The boundary maps satisfy ∂n ∂n+1 = 0 for each n, equivalently Im ∂n+1 ⊂ Ker ∂n, so (···→Cn+1→Cn→Cn−1→···) is a chain complex.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Lemma 2.1 style sign-cancellation arguments for simplicial/singular simplices to verify ∂^2=0; this ensures that boundaries are cycles and homology groups (Ker/Im) are well-defined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of n-cycles and n-boundaries
rubrics_metrics.description: In a chain complex, n-cycles are elements of Ker ∂n and n-boundaries are elements of Im ∂n+1; homology classes are cycles modulo boundaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practically, identify cycles by solving ∂(chain)=0 and identify which of these are boundaries (images of higher-dimensional chains) to compute Hn.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicial homology groups Hn(X)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a D-complex or simplicial complex X, define Cn(X) as free abelian on open n-simplices and Hn(X)=Ker ∂n / Im ∂n+1 (simplicial homology).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simplicial homology is efficient for complexes built from simplices; for general cell complexes use cellular or singular methods. Examples (S^1, torus, RP^2, S^n) illustrate computations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Singular homology definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Singular homology: Cn(X) is the free abelian group on all continuous maps σ:Δ^n→X (singular n-simplices) and ∂n is defined by the same alternating-face formula; Hn(X)=Ker ∂n / Im ∂n+1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Singular homology applies to all spaces (not just complexes). Although Cn(X) is huge, quotients Hn(X) are often manageable. For complexes, singular homology coincides with simplicial/cellular homology via the singular complex S(X).

rubrics_metrics.name: Homeomorphism invariance of singular homology
rubrics_metrics.description: Homeomorphic spaces have isomorphic singular homology groups Hn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because singular simplices compose with homeomorphisms, homeomorphisms induce isomorphisms on Cn and hence on Hn.

rubrics_metrics.name: Homotopy invariance (homotopy equivalence implies isomorphic homology)
rubrics_metrics.description: A map f:X→Y induces f_*:Hn(X)→Hn(Y) for each n, and f_* is an isomorphism if f is a homotopy equivalence (so homotopy equivalent spaces have isomorphic homology groups).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This fundamental property will be proved by constructing induced maps on chains and using chain homotopies; it underlies many applications (homotopy invariants).

rubrics_metrics.name: H0 and path-component splitting
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is nonempty and path-connected then H0(X) ≈ Z; in general H0(X) is a direct sum of Z's, one for each path-component of X (and C0/Im ∂1 maps to Z via augmentation ε).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the augmentation ε: C0→Z (sum of coefficients) to see that Ker ε = Im ∂1 when X is path-connected; this yields H0≈Z. Thus H0 counts path-components algebraically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduced homology and augmentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Define the augmentation ε:C0(X)→Z by ε(∑ n_i σ_i)=∑ n_i; the reduced homology groups Ĥn(X) are the homology groups of the augmented chain complex ···→C1→C0→Z→0, making a point have trivial homology in all dimensions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reduced homology when convenient to avoid special-casing H0; Ĥn(X) ≈ Hn(X) for n>0 and Ĥ0(X) fits into H0(X)⊕Z relationship described.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometric interpretation of cycles via finite complexes
rubrics_metrics.description: A singular n-chain ξ (with ±1 coefficients) can be assembled into a finite D-complex K_ξ by identifying faces corresponding to canceling boundary terms; if ξ is a cycle, K_ξ is an (oriented away-from-(n−3)-skeleton) manifold-like object and induces a map K_ξ→X representing the homology class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This constructs geometric representatives: H1 classes by oriented loops, H2 by maps of closed oriented surfaces; not all higher homology classes come from manifolds but this gives useful intuition and representatives for low dimensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples as computation templates
rubrics_metrics.description: Worked examples: S^1 has H0≈Z and H1≈Z (others zero); torus T with one-vertex cell structure gives H0≈Z, H1≈Z⊕Z (generated by [a],[b]), H2≈Z (generated by U−L); RP^2 yields H0≈Z, H1≈Z/2, H2=0; S^n from two n-simplices gives Hn≈Z.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use minimal cell/simplicial decompositions to compute chain groups and boundaries explicitly, then compute Ker/Im to obtain homology. These examples illustrate how attaching cells kills or creates homology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence of simplicial and singular homology for complexes
rubrics_metrics.description: For reasonable complexes (D-complexes/simplicial complexes), the singular homology Hn(X) coincides with the simplicial homology computed from a combinatorial decomposition (and simplicial complexes can be obtained by subdividing D-complexes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This justifies computing homology using simplicial or cellular chains for spaces admitting such structures; singular homology provides the general theory and guarantees invariance under homeomorphism/homotopy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of boundaries removing holes
rubrics_metrics.description: Attaching an n+1-cell whose boundary is a given n-cycle maps that cycle into Im ∂_{n+1}, so filling a hole reduces Hn (example: adding a 2-cell along a−b makes the cycle a−b a boundary, reducing H1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the chain-complex viewpoint: Im ∂_{n+1} are those cycles that bound higher-dimensional chains; attaching cells corresponds algebraically to enlarging Im ∂ and thus killing homology classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical computation tools referenced
rubrics_metrics.description: Cellular homology and Mayer–Vietoris sequences are presented (later) as efficient techniques for computing homology groups, with cellular homology leveraging cell structure and Mayer–Vietoris analogous to van Kampen for decompositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When direct simplicial/singular computations are large or unwieldy, switch to cellular homology (homology defined in terms of cellular chains) or Mayer–Vietoris for spaces decomposed into simpler pieces.
